A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EgoCogNav and the same CEN dataset. All pages, equations, tables and figures were readable through extraction and visual inspection. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original trajectory, head-motion and perceived-uncertainty experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations and behavioral analyses in Section 5 and Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments for the revised model, including baseline comparisons, cognitive-component ablations and behavior-specific forecasting results in Section 5 and Tables 1–4.

M1.justification: V2 replaces cross-attention fusion and uncertainty-weighted goal interpolation with independently encoded, pooled late fusion, learnable navigation-pattern memory and uncertainty-conditioned adaptive normalization. The auxiliary environment/behavior classifiers and their loss disappear from the architecture and total objective.

E1.justification: Both versions use CEN: approximately six hours, 17 participants, 226k RGB frames and 42 indoor/outdoor sites. The trajectory, head-motion and uncertainty tasks remain unchanged. V2's behavior-specific ablations use existing annotations rather than introducing new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the uncertainty comparison by adapting M_Transformer and EgoCast to predict uncertainty and reporting their MAE and correlation in Table 1. V1 evaluated these methods only for trajectory/head motion and compared uncertainty against EMU and PATH_U. The named motion comparators and dedicated uncertainty baselines remain.

E3.justification: Reported training changes from 200 to 300 epochs, batch size 16 to 64, maximum learning rate 5e-5 to 1e-4, and weight decay 1e-4 to 8e-5. Uncertainty evaluation adds high-uncertainty-subset MAE/correlation and removes event precision. New ablations introduce full-set, high-uncertainty and behavior-stratified component comparisons.

E4.justification: V1's auxiliary-loss, trajectory-loss and input-modality ablations are replaced by uncertainty-supervision, decoding and memory ablations in v2 Table 3. V2 Table 4 adds component comparisons within annotated behaviors, while v1's per-behavior mean-uncertainty/effect-size analysis disappears. The qualitative examples and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: V1 reports standardized behavioral effect sizes in Tables 2 and 3; v2 removes these statistical summaries. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The predicted perceived-uncertainty values are task outputs, not statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Many results change beyond rounding. Full-set EgoCogNav ADE/FDE changes from 0.12/0.22 to 0.1051/0.2074, while Const_Vel FDE changes from 0.33 to 0.4257. EgoCogNav uncertainty MAE/correlation changes from 0.23/0.64 to 0.0986/0.788. New component and behavior-specific results replace earlier entries. Changed model and training settings prevent interpreting these as isolated same-setting gains.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for memory retrieval, residual injection and adaptive normalization in Equations 2–4. The displayed head-rotation loss also changes from a predicted/target rotation product to a product with the target transpose, correcting v1 Equation 3 in v2 Equation 6. No theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain joint cognition-aware forecasting, the CEN dataset, behavioral association and generalization to unseen environments. V2 removes the introduction's specific claim that auxiliary environment/behavior predictors provide stability and generalization, consistent with their removal from the method.

C2.justification: V2 replaces interpretations centered on auxiliary regularization and trajectory-loss benefits with explanations involving gradient coupling, modality-specific late fusion and complementary memory/decoding effects. It also interprets heuristic uncertainty baselines as insufficient for subjective, person-specific uncertainty. The existing occlusion, single-future and short-horizon limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 specifies model width 512, four action-encoder layers, two perception-encoder layers, 16 memory slots of width 256, and initialization/activation details. These expand implementation documentation beyond the revised training settings. The single RTX 4090, frozen cached DINOv2 features and data-processing pipeline remain; no new code or dataset access instructions appear.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a focused memory-augmented prediction discussion covering MemoNet, MTR++, trajectory anchors and ReMoDiffuse, positioning cognition-conditioned processing relative to these approaches. Additional citations support adaptive normalization, SiLU and the forecasting timescale. Most existing navigation, cognition and dataset positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The method exposition is substantially reorganized into fusion, cognition subcomponents, prediction and a separate Training Objectives subsection. Quantitative results and ablation explanations are extensively rewritten. Contributions are reformatted and notation/grammar refined, although much of the introduction, dataset description, qualitative discussion and limitations remains.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, Figure 2 is redrawn for the revised architecture, and the tables receive substantially different columns and organization. Figure 4 rearranges the same failure examples side by side. Figures 1 and 3 retain their artwork, with changes in scale and placement.

improvement.justification: V2 makes the central cognitive mechanism more assessable through direct component ablations, learned uncertainty comparators and clearer implementation details. These provide a net evidentiary improvement over v1. The gain is tempered by removing modality/loss checks and behavioral effect-size summaries; changed training settings and continued absence of repeated-run reporting also limit conclusions from the revised scores.
